197.title: Vayishlach: three ways to prepare
197.hook: Rashi: Jacob readied gifts, prayer and defense before meeting Esau
197.howItsDone: Jewish teachers cite Rashi's three preparations, gift, prayer and defense, as a guide for facing conflict, and the chapter is read each late autumn in Vayishlach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, katonti, and Jacob's prayer. Your line was too small for all this kindness. Today, the night before the meeting.

The night before the big interview. The surgery. The hard talk with your landlord, or your father. Some people only worry. Some only pray. Some only make spreadsheets. Jacob has a brother coming toward him with four hundred men, and one night to get ready. Read the chapter closely and he does three very different things. Rashi, centuries later, gave the pattern a name.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `WORRY, PRAY, OR PLAN?` → `JACOB DOES THREE THINGS.`

segments.voice: Rashi says Jacob prepared himself for three things: for a gift, for prayer, and for war. Take them one at a time. War, or really, defense. Jacob divides his people and flocks into two camps. If Esau attacks one, the other can escape. He isn't planning to fight his brother. He's planning so that not everyone is lost. Prayer: we heard it yesterday. God of my fathers, I'm too small for all your kindness; save me, I'm afraid. And a gift. Jacob sets aside hundreds of animals: goats and sheep, rams, camels with their young, cows and bulls, donkeys. He sends them ahead in separate droves, each with its own servant, and tells them: put space between one drove and the next. So Esau meets gift after gift after gift, each servant saying, this is a present for my lord Esau, from your servant Jacob. The Hebrew for the gift is minchah, the same word as the afternoon prayer, Mincha. A gift to a brother and a gift to God share a name. Jacob explains his plan in a phrase that's hard to translate. Literally: I will cover his face with the gift. Some hear in it the root of kapparah, atonement, the covering-over of a wrong. Read that way, Jacob isn't only buying safety. He's trying to repay, a little, what he took twenty years ago. Teachers draw a lesson from Rashi's three: facing something hard, you don't have to pick just one. Generosity, prayer for those who pray, and plain good sense can work together.

segments.voice: Hold one hard thing coming up this week, and find one sensible step you could take, and one gift or kind word you could offer the other person. Then, if you pray, bring it to God; if you don't, take one quiet breath with it, and let all three sit together.

198.title: Vayishlach: the limp (Genesis 32:32–33)
198.hook: Jacob limps from the wrestling, and Jews still avoid eating the sinew of the thigh
198.howItsDone: Kosher butchers remove the gid hanasheh, the sciatic nerve, from the hindquarter in a skilled process called nikkur, and in some places the hindquarters are simply not sold as kosher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gift, a prayer and two camps. Your line was prepare three ways. Today, what happened that night.

An old injury can go quiet for months. A knee from a bike crash, a wrist that never quite healed right. Then one cold morning it aches, and the day it came from comes back with it. The night before meeting Esau, Jacob is alone by the river Jabbok, and a man wrestles with him until dawn. Jacob won't let go without a blessing, and he walks away with a new name, Israel. He also walks away with something else.
screen: `THE OLD ACHE ON A COLD MORNING.` → `WRESTLING UNTIL DAWN.` → `A NEW NAME, AND SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: During the struggle, the man touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and it was wrenched. Jacob names the place Peniel, face of God, because, he says, I have seen God face to face, and I'm still alive. Then the Torah gives us a picture. The sun rose on him as he passed Peniel, and he was limping on his thigh. Morning light, a new name, and a limp. He isn't the same man who crossed the river. Then the Torah does something unusual: it steps out of the story to speak to the future. Therefore, it says, the children of Israel don't eat the sinew of the thigh, on the hollow of the thigh, to this day, because he touched Jacob's thigh there. In Hebrew, that sinew is the gid hanasheh. Tradition identifies it with the sciatic nerve, which runs down the back of the leg. And the practice is real. Jewish law forbids eating it, and there's a whole chapter of the Mishnah about it. Removing it from the hindquarter of an animal is slow, skilled work, and in some places kosher butchers find it simpler not to use the hindquarters at all. So one night by a river still shapes what's on the table, generations of dinners later. Why remember the limp, and not only the victory? A medieval book on the commandments says it's a sign: Jacob struggled, was hurt, and wasn't defeated. His children would struggle too, and endure. The limp isn't a shame to hide. It's a memory the body keeps, on purpose, so the story doesn't get lost.

segments.voice: Find a scar, on your body or one that doesn't show: a loss, a failure, a hard year, and put your hand on it if you can. Remember the night it came from: you wrestled, you were hurt, and you're still here. Don't rush to fix the memory; let it be part of your story, the way the limp is part of Jacob's.

199.title: Vayishlach: back to Bethel (Genesis 35:1–15)
199.hook: Jacob buries the old idols and returns to where he dreamed
199.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats fulfilling vows seriously, and on Yom Kippur eve the Kol Nidre service opens by addressing unfulfilled vows; Jacob's return to Bethel is read in Vayishlach each late autumn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gid hanasheh, and Jacob limping into the sunrise. Your line was the limp remembers. Today, Jacob goes back to where it started.

Maybe you've driven past the house you grew up in. Or walked into the old school gym, or the hospital chapel where you once made a promise. The place looks smaller. You're older. And you remember who you were, and what you said you'd do. Jacob has met Esau; they've embraced and gone their separate ways. His family has been through a violent, painful chapter in the town of Shechem. Now God speaks: go up to Bethel. The place of the ladder.
screen: `THE HOUSE YOU GREW UP IN.` → `A HARD CHAPTER AT SHECHEM.` → `GO UP TO BETHEL.`

segments.voice: Go up to Bethel, God says, live there, and make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother. Remember that night? The stone for a pillow, the ladder, the vow. Jacob doesn't just pack. First he turns to his household and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Put away the strange gods that are among you." Purify yourselves, change your clothes. Wait. Strange gods, in Jacob's camp? The Torah has been hinting. When the family left Laban's house, Rachel secretly took her father's household idols. After Shechem there was plunder, too. Somewhere in those tents and saddlebags, the old gods came along. So the family hands them over, the idols and the earrings they wore, and Jacob buries them under the great tree near Shechem. He doesn't smash them in public. He buries them, and leaves them behind. Then they go up. Along the way Deborah, Rebekah's old nurse, dies, and they bury her under an oak they name the oak of weeping. At Bethel, God appears again, blesses Jacob, and repeats his new name: Israel. And Jacob does exactly what he did twenty years before: he sets up a stone pillar and pours oil on it. Same place, same stone ritual, different man. The rabbis read Bethel as the promise kept. Jacob vowed there, if God would bring him home in peace. Now he's back, keeping his side. But first, he had to bury what he'd been carrying that didn't belong.

200.title: Vayishlach: Esau's family (Genesis 35:29–36:43)
200.hook: the brothers bury Isaac together, and Esau's descendants are listed with care
200.howItsDone: The genealogy of Esau is read aloud in synagogues each year as part of Vayishlach, every name included, and Jewish teachers point to Deuteronomy's command not to abhor an Edomite.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bethel, and a family burying its idols under a tree. Your line was bury the old gods. And this is day two hundred: two hundred days on the path. Today, a chapter that's easy to skip.

At a family reunion, there's always the other side. The cousins from your uncle's marriage, the ones you see once every five years. Different town, different jokes, different photos on the fridge. You're polite. You don't really know their story. Genesis 36 is that other side of the family: a long list of names, easy to let your eyes slide right over. But it comes right after a funeral, and it's there on purpose.
screen: `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE FAMILY.` → `GENESIS 36: A LIST OF NAMES.` → `THERE ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the funeral. Isaac dies at a hundred and eighty, old and full of days, and the text says his sons Esau and Jacob buried him. When Abraham died, Isaac was named before Ishmael. Here the older brother, Esau, comes first. The two brothers who fought in the womb, and over a blessing, stand together at their father's grave. Then the Torah turns, not to Jacob, but to Esau. These are the generations of Esau, who is Edom: his wives, his sons, his grandsons. Esau moved his whole household to the hill country of Seir, because the land couldn't hold both brothers' flocks. No war, no curse. They just needed room. Then come chiefs, and a list of the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. Esau's family had kings first, and the Torah says so, calmly. One name in the list caught the rabbis' eye: Timna. The Talmud tells a story about her. She wanted to join Abraham's family and was turned away, so she became the concubine of Esau's son instead, and from her descended Amalek, later Israel's enemy. The rabbis' lesson: be careful whom you push away. Later the Torah says it plainly, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite, for he is thy brother." God gave Esau his land too, Deuteronomy says, and Israel was told not to fight over it. A whole chapter for the brother who wasn't chosen, every name written down with care.

201.title: Vayeshev: wanting to settle (Genesis 37:1)
201.hook: Rashi: Jacob wished to live in peace, and Joseph's troubles sprang upon him
201.howItsDone: Vayeshev is read in synagogues in early winter, often near Hanukkah, and Rashi's comment on Jacob's wish for tranquility is taught alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a whole chapter for Esau's family. Your line was his story matters too. Today, a new portion, and Jacob wants to sit down.

The move is done, the boxes are unpacked, the kids are finally sleeping through the night. You sit down on the couch and think: now, finally, calm. That's usually when the phone rings. Jacob's life has been like a storm. A brother who wanted him dead. Twenty years with a difficult uncle. Wrestling, limping, burying his mother's nurse, and his beloved Rachel. Now he's home. This portion is called Vayeshev, and he settled.
screen: `FINALLY, THE COUCH.` → `A LIFE LIKE A STORM.` → `VAYESHEV: AND HE SETTLED.`

segments.voice: It opens with a quiet verse: Jacob settled in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan. Notice the two verbs. His father Isaac sojourned there, lived like a guest. Jacob wants to settle, to sit down, to stay. The very next verse starts the story of Joseph: a seventeen-year-old, a favorite son, a coat, some dreams, and brothers who hate him. Within a chapter, Joseph is gone and Jacob is tearing his clothes in grief. Rashi, reading those two verses side by side, drew on an old midrash. Jacob wished to dwell in tranquility, he says, and the troubles of Joseph sprang upon him. Then a sharp line: the righteous want to live at ease in this world too, and God says, isn't what's waiting for them in the world to come enough? That can sound harsh. But Rashi isn't mocking the wish for peace. He's noticing a pattern in the text. One way to hear it: calm is real, but it isn't a place you move into and own. It comes, and it goes. Hard years are still ahead of Jacob, and some of his sweetest too. In the end, he'll see Joseph again. Vayeshev comes from the same root as yeshivah, a place where you sit and study, and as the word for sitting in a home. Jewish life has plenty of sitting: at the Shabbat table, in study, even in mourning, when a family sits shivah, the seven days, low to the ground. Jewish life treats rest as holy. The text just never promises it will last.

segments.voice: Notice any calm there is right now, even a little: the chair holding you, the quiet in the room, or the noise you've gotten used to, and enjoy it without clutching. Then let yourself know it will change, and that you've come through changes before. Hold both: this rest is real, and it doesn't have to last forever to be good.

202.title: Vayeshev: the man in the field (Genesis 37:15–17)
202.hook: a nameless stranger points Joseph to his brothers; midrash calls him an angel
202.howItsDone: Joseph's words, et achai anochi mevakesh, I seek my brothers, are quoted in Jewish teaching and song as a call to look for and care for one another.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayeshev: Jacob wanting to settle, and trouble springing up. Your line was rest comes and goes. Today, Joseph goes looking for his brothers.

You're lost in a new city. Your phone is dead. You've walked the same block three times. Then someone, an old man at a bus stop, a kid on a bike, asks: you look lost, where are you trying to go? Two sentences later you're on your way, and you never see them again. Joseph's brothers are far from home, grazing the flocks. Jacob sends Joseph, alone, to check on them. He goes to Shechem, where they were supposed to be. They aren't there.
screen: `LOST, PHONE DEAD.` → `SENT TO FIND HIS BROTHERS.` → `THEY AREN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: The Torah says a man found Joseph wandering in the field. Just, a man. No name. He asks, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "What seekest thou?" Joseph answers, in Hebrew: et achai anochi mevakesh. "I seek my brethren." Tell me, please, where they're pasturing. The stranger says: they've moved on. I heard them say, let's go to Dothan. So Joseph goes to Dothan, the brothers see him coming, and the story turns. The pit, the caravan, Egypt: everything that follows starts with a stranger who knew where they'd gone. Why does the Torah bother with him? Three verses for a man with no name, who asks one question and gives one answer. The commentators each give an answer. An old midrash, which Rashi quotes, says the man was the angel Gabriel. Ramban, in medieval Spain, said: whether or not he was an angel, the point is that Joseph's story had to happen, and when Joseph was about to give up and go home, someone was put in his path. Others read him as simply a passerby, which may be the point too. The text itself doesn't say who he was. It only tells us that when Joseph was lost, somebody noticed, asked, and pointed. A life can have figures like that too. A teacher who mentioned a book. A stranger who gave a name, a number, a direction. Their names slip away, and the thanks go unsaid.

203.title: Vayeshev: the empty pit (Genesis 37:24)
203.hook: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it"
203.howItsDone: The sale of Joseph is read in synagogues each winter in Vayeshev, and later Jewish tradition links the brothers' sin to the martyrdom of ten sages remembered on Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man with no name who pointed Joseph to Dothan. Your line was someone points the way. This week: three ways to prepare, a limp, back to Bethel, Esau's family, wanting to settle, and the man in the field. Today, what waited at Dothan.

Some moments in life are just a hole. A diagnosis. A layoff. The night the house goes quiet after a divorce. You're at the bottom of something, and you can't see a way up. Joseph walks toward his brothers across the fields at Dothan, wearing the coat his father gave him. They see him coming from far off. Before he reaches them, they've already made a plan.
screen: `AT THE BOTTOM OF SOMETHING.` → `THE COAT, SEEN FROM FAR OFF.` → `A PLAN BEFORE HE ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Here comes the dreamer, they say. Let's kill him, throw him into one of the pits, and say a wild animal ate him. Then we'll see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the oldest, steps in. Don't take his life. Throw him into this pit, here in the wilderness, but don't lay a hand on him. The Torah tells us why: Reuben meant to come back later and rescue him. So Joseph arrives, and they strip off his coat, the coat, and throw him into the pit. Then one flat detail, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and the pit was empty, there was no water in it." Why tell us that? If it's empty, of course there's no water. The rabbis read the doubled phrase slowly. The Talmud says: there was no water in it, but there were snakes and scorpions. Empty of what helps, and not empty of what harms. Others hear it more plainly. It was a cistern for catching rain, and it was dry, so Joseph wouldn't drown. Empty can be terrible. It can also be the thing that keeps you alive. Then the next verse, flat and cold: the brothers sat down to eat bread. Their brother is in a hole nearby, and they have lunch. The story doesn't let us look away from that. Joseph is in the pit, stripped, alone, nothing in it but darkness. And, the story will show, it isn't the end of him.
screen: `HERE COMES THE DREAMER.` · `REUBEN: DON'T KILL HIM.` · `NO WATER, BUT SNAKES AND SCORPIONS.` · `THEY SAT DOWN TO EAT.` · then, large: `THE PIT WAS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Where is there a dry pit in your life right now: a friendship that went quiet, a hope that ran out, a hole where a person used to be? Don't rush to fill it; just look at it honestly. Is it only empty, or is there something in there too, fear, or strength you didn't know you had?
